label: Cream
comment: Cream as it is sold, its fat set to a grade and heated: each country names its own grades, hung under the ruler at the least fat the name allows (or, where it sets none, what it usually has); what is made from it branches off to its right.

about.text: Cream is a dairy product composed of the higher-fat layer skimmed from the top of milk before homogenization. The butterfat, which is less dense, rises to the top and is skimmed off, resulting in gravity cream. The industrial production of cream instead uses centrifugal separators to make separator cream. Cream is often sold in grades defined by their butterfat content. It contains high levels of saturated fat, in ascending proportion from light cream to heavy cream.

sources.text: All the raw cream, pasteurised: about 5.5 Mt sold as cream (about 2.5 Mt in the EU: Germany 0.52, France 0.47, Belgium 0.27, Poland 0.26; 0.3 Mt in the UK; as much again elsewhere), the rest churned into butter and ghee and made into ice cream, cream cheese and the rest.

how.text: The cream spun out of the milk is far richer than any grade sold, so the dairy blends it back with skimmed milk until the fat hits the legal figure, then heats it. Grades differ by country and by use: coffee, whipping, double. Cream is heated like milk, but because fat shields bacteria it is held a little hotter once it reaches 10 % fat. Equivalent time-temperature pairs are allowed; the figures are the US legal definitions (21 CFR 131.3).

steps.note: Cream and skimmed milk are mixed back to the fat of the grade.
Alternatively a batch (vat) at 63 °C for 30 min, 3 °C hotter from 10 % fat up, or ultra-pasteurised at 138 °C or more for 2 s or more, which keeps longer.
